nodes.label: Humanities in a Changing Climate
nodes.notes: **2017-2018** The projects in this cohort were developed around the question "what is the work of the humanities in a changing climate?" In its narrowest interpretation, it called for collaborative work on climate change, arguably the most pressing grand challenge of our time. As a metaphor, climate change is pluripotent: it offers humanists the opportunity to think expansively about the meanings of "climate" and "change" as they manifest in their own research, and to bring their contributions to bear on cognate questions in the present.

nodes.label: Hmong Memory at the Crossroads
nodes.notes: **Hmong Memory at the Crossroads" and "Growing Up Hmong at the Crossroads** Conceived as a cross-institutional, transnational and campus-community partnership, this documentary weaves oral histories of three generations of Hmong refugees in the Midwest, France and Thailand as they retrace their roots in Laos, bringing into the critical spotlight unknown episodes of their fraught history, linked to their combat alongside theFrench and American armies during the French-Indochina War (1945-54) and the American Secret War in Laos (1961-75). Set in three continents, these testimonials are emotional events originating from a place of trauma, loss and suffering, but also of healing and redemption, to repair lives and rebuild communities devastated by past conflicts.

nodes.label: A History of World Music Recording
nodes.notes: **A History of World Music Recording** This project combines research in audio archives at the University of Chicago, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, and the University of Wisconsin-Madison to document the circulation of recorded world music, which began in the Midwest in the 1890s before spreading throughout the world during the twentieth century. Three collaborative symposia, digitizing projects, and a library exhibit that travels to each university will produce three publications, each containing two compact discs of historical recordings and an accompanying books, audibly connecting the Midwest to the politics and culture of world music in the global twenty-first century.

nodes.label: Aggregating Great Lakes Environmental History
nodes.notes:
**Aggregating Great Lakes Environmental History: Exploring the Value of Distributed Digital Archives for Research and Teaching** This project assembles a distributed thematic digital collection on the environmental history of the Great Lakes basin from the perspective of the land and its people. This project is an exploration of the value for research and teaching of assembling a digital thematic collection on the Great Lakes basin when scholars have neither specified what materials are digitized nor directed the assembly of diverse
digitized collections into an aggregated whole. The Principal Investigator will create three partnership models and weave them into a single holistic experiment on emerging digital research.  One model is working relationships with two humanities faculty (History and English) in at the University of Illinois who share a research interest in environmental history in the Midwest and a commitment to exploring digital forms of primary resources. The second model is the assembly of digital content from at least four independent digital archives in CIC+ universities. The third partnership model is an alliance with the Advanced Research Collaborative at Texas A&M University, which is making available a mature and
robust technology platform for assembling a distributed digital research collections. The heart of the project is understanding, evaluating, and reporting on the experience of collaborating faculty (and their students in multiple courses) in discovering, retrieving, and utilizing the digital documents from the aggregated collection.

nodes.notes: **The Great Lakes and the Global Midwest" and "Great Lakes and the Jordan Valley: Articulating Water Needs, the Right to Water, and Water Sovereignty in the Quest for Water Justice** At this unique moment of radically changing water geography, we propose to establish a multisite Great Lakes Lab rooted in the Humanities and Social Sciences. The Lab will generate curricula, conferences, and innovative research projects that bridge campus and community. Participants in Great Lakes Lab events will approach issues of water distribution, toxicity, and privatization from a social angle and propose policy, as well as grassroots, initiatives. Funding from the Global Midwest initiative will enable us to seed the Lab at the University of Illinois at Chicago, Michigan State University, and the University of Michigan.

nodes.label: The Midwaste
nodes.notes: **The Midwaste: Midwestern Wasteways and Global Futures** This project builds a cross-campus initiative to build an academic infrastructure for humanities-based teaching, research, and public engagement in waste studies. As a region where the national production, global circulation, and local accumulation of waste clash with histories of economic growth and visions for sustainable global futures, the American Midwest is an ideal location to develop such an infrastructure. This project lays the groundwork for a permanent institute for waste studies through the establishment of a web portal, development of cross-campus teaching modules, and organization of a multi-disciplinary symposium.

nodes.label: Perform Midwest
nodes.notes: **Perform Midwest: Incubating Collaborative Research** This project brings together three teams of scholars, artists, and students to work on shared arts practice as a form of humanistic inquiry. Through as series of developmental residencies, project participants consider how the arts foster public engagement and create linkages between the academy and local communities. The project lays ground for a Mid-Western network of artist / humanist collaborations that address research questions emerging from the Midwest, but are global in scope. Project outcomes are public performances, a digital archive, and a performance catalog with scholar commentary.

nodes.label: Muslims of the Midwest
nodes.notes: **Muslims of the Midwest: An Oral History Project** Despite the significant history of Muslim presence in “the heartland,” there has been relatively little oral and visual historical documentation of Midwestern Muslims. The primary goal of the present project is to establish and build a digital archive that documents the varied experiences of American Muslims in the Midwest through testimonies across generational, gender, geographical, socio-economic, and ethnic differences. The desired outcome is a digital archive that would serve as (1) primary source material for scholarly research and (2) material for instructional use for schools and colleges.

nodes.label: African Immigration and the Production of the Global Futures
nodes.notes:
**African Immigration and the Production of the Global Futures: Detroit and Berlin** Building on the original proposal, "African Immigrants and the Production of the Global Midwest: Detroit and Minneapolis," the revised project will move the focus from Detroit and Minneapolis to Detroit and Berlin. It will think through the ways in which these two cities are global from the perspectives of African immigration, and African imaginations of global futures. Berlin will help to elucidate what is distinctive about Detroit and vise versa. What, we will ask, are the distinctions between how African futures can be imagined in Europe versus the U.S., in Detroit versus Berlin? How do race, citizenship, and humanitarian projects work in relation to African immigration in these two cities? What difference do the approaches to urban planning,districting, education, and social versus capital networks make? What kinds of communities are formed? How do "Africans" relate to "Blackness" versus "foreignness" in both cities? What difference does it make when one is a noncitizen?

*Original Project Description* Our collaborative research team will investigate how African immigrants forged an urban global Midwest since the 1980s, focusing on the strikingly divergent cases of the Twin Cities and Detroit. We will track how strife in Africa in the 1990s produced a profusion of humanitarian and refugee services in these cities; and open critical dialogue about race, mobility, and African aspirations in our unevenly globalized Midwest. Using mixed, comparative, and participatory methods, we will investigate African shaping spaces and livelihoods, founding transnational Black businesses, and challenging their portrayal as needy victims.

nodes.label: "There There"
nodes.notes: ***There There*: A Journal of Global Contemporary Art in the Midwest** This project will develop an online journal of contemporary global art focused on works exhibited, and in some cases made, in the Midwestern United States. In addition to regular exhibition reviews and interviews, the journal will also host conferences on, and publish longer critical essays about, issues related to the Midwest as a global center for ongoing artistic activity. This journal will fill the current gap in art reporting and criticism in the Midwest.

nodes.label: The Importance of the Last Generation
nodes.notes: **The Importance of the Last Generation: Midwest Heritage German Speakers** The Midwest is remarkable for the massive numbers of German-speaking immigrants who settled here from the 1830s onward. Communities often remained in large part monolingual in German for several generations and thousands today still speak some kind of German. These ‘good old immigrants’ offer an opportunity to discuss pressing issues of immigrant bilingualism from new perspectives, including the cognitive advantages of bilingualism and immigrant language policies. This proposal seeks funding (1) to work with graduate students in producing new research on these communities and (2) to bring our findings to a broad public and policy makers.
nodes.info: **PI**: Michael T. Putnam *(Penn State University)* **Co-PI**: Joseph Salmons *(University of Wisconsin-Madison)*

nodes.label: Open Fields
nodes.notes: **Open Fields: The Chicago Field Museum's Anthropology Collection and Its Influence on European Enchantments with Native America** This project considers the global impact that Chicago’s Field Museum has had on Euro-American understandings of Indigenous peoples and contemporary debates around their cultural property rights. Open Fields revisits the Museum’s 1896 expedition to the Hopi Tribe to track how, from Arizona’s deserts, a small Puebloan culture could influence some of Europe’s leading 20th century humanists. Collaborators from four universities (including two HWW Consortium members), three museums, and the Hopi Cultural Preservation Office will take up this history as both a genealogy of today’s Indigenous cultural politics and its potential for sparking new partnerships between Native nations and ethnographic museums.
nodes.info: **PI**: Justin B. Richland *(University of Chicago)*, **Co-PIs**: Alaka Wali *(Field Museum of Natural History)*, Frederick Hoxie *(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign)*

nodes.label: The Religious Soundmap Project of the Global Midwest
nodes.notes: **The Religious Soundmap Project of the Global Midwest** What does religion in the Global Midwest sound like? This question animates the Religious Soundmap Project, which will invite broad public audiences to experience the religious diversity of the Midwest through sound. Student researchers will produce audio recordings of religion “in practice.” These recordings will be edited, archived, and integrated, along with interviews, visual images, explanatory texts, and interpretive essays, onto a publicly accessible online mapping platform. This innovative digital humanities project will provide new research and pedagogical tools for scholars, experiential learning opportunities for students, and an interactive resource for the general public.
nodes.info: **PI**: Isaac Weiner *(The Ohio State University)* **Co-PI**: Amy DeRogatis *(Michigan State University)*

nodes.label: 'BlackLivesMatter'
nodes.notes: **'BlackLivesMatter': Racial Tension and Police Violence in the Midwest and Beyond** This project utilizes humanistic methods to address the relationship between race, grassroots activism, and state-sponsored violence through examing how Blacks in the Midwest have (re)created Black identities and ideas of Blackness that have national and global impact. Specifically, we focus on responses to the 2014 death of Michael Brown and the protests in Ferguson, Missouri by examining the responses of Black lawmakers in Missouri to state-sponsored violence. We also examine the reverberations of Black political grassroots activism in the wake of the events of Ferguson abroad by focusing on how Black populations in France relate the events of Ferguson

nodes.label: ¡Latinoamérica Presente!
nodes.notes: ***¡Latinoamérica Presente!*: Tracing the Hidden Histories of Latina/o Art, Aesthetics, and Expressive Culture in the Global Midwest** This project examines the role of arts and music in advancing collective social expression in Chicago, South Bend, Omaha, and Columbus. It utilizes various strategies to interpret the unique global Midwest complexities of transnational experiences—migratory processes, bi-national identities, and transnational networks—focusing on ways by which artistic expressions in the visual and musical arts have illuminated and communicated social realities that speak to the Midwest's becoming global in Latino context.

nodes.label: Collaborative Innovation and the Global Midwest
nodes.notes: **Collaboration Innovation and the Global Midwest: Inter-disciplinary Design and Envisioning Prairie Futures** This collaboration takes a cross-disciplinary, multi-campus coordinated exploration into the Midwest's layered innovation histories that have often been overshadowed by innovation narratives focused on dominant regions and centers of computing (whether academic sites like MIT or Stanford, or regions like Silicon Valley and Massachusetts' Route 128). This research collaboration adopts a distinct approach to innovation studies by looking to shed light on interdisciplinary digital developments in the Midwest – from educational and public computing, to electroacoustic design – that necessarily bridged expertise from social sciences, natural sciences, engineering, and humanities; and that have frequently been overlooked, even as they have played roles in reshaping global disciplinary imaginaries, markets, and ecologies. We propose a strategy to develop a means to extend research and pedagogical resources – both existing and proposed, and both physical and digital – to expand greater visibility of such local, multi-disciplinary histories around collaborative regional innovation.

nodes.label: The Earth Will Not Abide
nodes.notes: **The Earth Will Not Abide** Fields Hands Plows Shares is a documentary project that depicts a world in which seeds and soil become financial abstractions and humans become elements in mechanized supply chains. Fields... will specifically focus on the cross-continental relationships between the grain fields of the US, Brazil, and Argentina--geographies reshaped by automation and global trade. The project questions the ecological and social viability of this system while exploring both traditional and emerging alternatives. Combining audio-visual documents (video, photographs, creative maps) and critical writing, it will conclude with a digital publication and a public exhibition and series of events.
nodes.info: **PI**: Ryan Griffis *(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign)* **Co-PIs**: Lorelei Stewart *(University of Illinois Chicago)*, Claire Pentecost *(artist)*, Brett Hanover *(filmmaker)*

nodes.label: Insurgent Midwest
nodes.notes: **Insurgent Midwest: Transformational Dialogue for a Humane Urbanism** This project focuses on the American Midwest as a site of locally situated but transnationally networked social movements that use insurgent practices to create more inclusive and humane cities. It assembles an engaged group of scholars, artists, and activists from UIUC, UIC, and two community-based movements in Chicago that have strong ties with similarly dispossessed communities waging struggles against eviction and marginalization in the global South— namely Mexico and South Africa. Through a series of transnational dialogue workshops, the project aims to produce knowledge about the insurgent Midwest by documenting in multimedia form the stories, struggles, and successes of transnationally networked social movements.
nodes.info: **PI**: Faranak Miraftab *(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign)* **Project Team**: Andy Clarno *(University of Illinois Chicago)*, Ken Salo *(UIUC)*, Stacy Harwood *(University of Utah, formerly UIUC)*, Marc Doussard *(UIUC)*, Iván Arenas *(UIC)*, Ryan Griffis *(UIUC)*, Efadul Huq *(Smith College, formerly UIUC)*, Mexico Solidarity Network, Chicago Anti-Eviction Campaign

nodes.label: Detroit in China
nodes.notes: **Detroit in China: Postindustrial Cities and Urban Representations in the Midwest and China** This research and publication project comparatively examines urban marginality in cities in the Midwest and China. Choosing Detroit and Harbin (northeast China) as fieldwork sites, we investigate uneven development and its representation in visual culture. Based on policy analyses. fieldwork interviews, and visual documentation, this project examines the processes and representations of deindustrialization in the Midwest and China, as well as the current policy experiments for urban revitalization. It will be among the first comparative studies on urban transformations in postindustrial U.S. and China, and contribute to our understanding on urban inequality in both the global South and North.
nodes.info: **PI**: Xuefei Ren *(Michigan State University)* **Co-PIs**: Tze-lan Sang *(MSU)*, Wendy Griswold *(Northwestern University)*, Yue Zhang *(University of Illinois Chicago)*

nodes.label: The New Ethics of Food
nodes.notes: **The New Ethics of Food** There is growing public recognition that the issues involved with the global food system pose complex challenges that require critical consideration. The purpose of the New Ethics of Food project is to reveal and rethink the Midwest as a major force in this century’s food economy and culture, and to demonstrate how the public humanities can contribute to this work. Outcomes will include the development of 1) a digital platform to serve as a visual representation of a Midwest food ethics research network, and 2) an interactive food ethics research focus within the online journal, The Public Philosophy Journal.

nodes.label: Performing History
nodes.notes: **Performing History: Documenting and Enacting the Asian American Midwest** As an interdisciplinary collaboration, “Performing History” brings together the practices of archival research, oral history research, literary textual analysis, creative writing, and dramatic performance, training community members to interpret and perform historical sources, such as oral history transcripts, personal recollections, letters, diaries, and other documentedrecollections of Asian Americans. Through these workshops and performances, we seek to foster a participatory public humanities that blurs boundaries between audience, performer, and researcher, thereby encouraging a broad sense of common endeavor and community. By presenting the voices of Asian Americans, the project will promote a redefinition of the Global Midwest.
nodes.info: **PI**: Ji-Yeon Yuh *(Northwestern University)* **Co-PIs**: David Furumoto *(University of Wisconsin-Madison)*, Timothy Yu *(UW-Madison)*, Victor Jew *(UW-Madison)*

nodes.label: Building Sustainable Worlds
nodes.notes: **Building Sustainable Worlds: Latinx Placemaking in the Midwest** This project launched an ambitious set of activities that involved field research, graduate student workshops, a symposium, “brainstorming” sessions with invited speakers, and the production of an edited volume. We regard this project as a continuation of the regional networkbuilding inaugurated through the Latina/o Midwest events held at the University of Iowa in 2012-13. This proposal brings arts and humanities perspectives to address the grant theme of “climate change,” as it encompasses cultural, political, social, and environmental factors affecting Latina/o communities in the Midwest. Among the questions we address are: How do Latinas/os in the Midwest create communities and environments to sustain themselves, often amidst culturally and socially hostile climates? How are Latinas/os, long drawn to the region for industrial andagricultural work, impacted by the physical and material climate and environments of the region? And how do Latinas/os transform their cultural and physical environments to create sustainable communities? Faculty and graduate student participants are divided into three working groups around the topics of historical and cultural sites; performance; and literature and film. We gathered on four occasions over 2017 and 2018 to discuss, present, and edit our research.
nodes.info: **PI**: Theresa Delgadillo *(The Ohio State University)* **Lead Organizers**: Geraldo Cadava *(Northwestern University)*, Claire Fox *(University of Iowa)*, Sonia BasSheva Mañjon *(Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts, formerly Barnett Center for Integrated Arts and Enterprise OSU)*, Ramón Rivera-Servera *(University of Texas-Austin, formerly Northwestern University)*

nodes.label: Legacies of the Enlightenment
nodes.notes: **Legacies of the Enlightenment: Humanity, Nature, and Science in a Changing Climate** Legacies of the Enlightenment responds to the question how the Enlightenment has come to inform our current concept of humanity and the interrelation of human and non-human. The period of the Enlightenment was a time when the boundaries separating organic and inorganic materials were beginning to crumble, but it was also a time in which the categories that define what constitutes a “normal” human were solidifying. The interrelation of human and non-human that we examine in this project defines how we comprehend, for example environmental pollution, social injustice, racism, sexual orientation, and how a monolithic definition of humanity is challenged by natural catastrophes and epidemics. In order to address these issues efficiently, we have assembled a team of scholars that cuts across disciplines, time periods, and institutions. This interdisciplinary configuration opens up the space for a dialogue on these topics. Our project will consist of a website where scholars and graduate students will collaborate on categories related to the interrelation of human and non-human. Furthermore, Legacies of the Enlightenment will organize a workshop where graduate students and faculty will present research related to the topics of our website, receive feedback, and revise their work into publishable articles.
nodes.info: **PI**: Valentina Denzel *(Michigan State University)* **Co-PI**: Tracy Rutler *(Penn State University)*

nodes.label: Crow
nodes.notes: **Crow: the Corpus and Repository of Writing** The changing climate in the humanities—increased use of technology and multimodal writing, greater participation of multilingual and multicultural students in U.S. universities, and economic and political pressure on humanities programs—demands new approaches to research, teaching, and mentoring. Crow, the Corpus and Repository of Writing, responds to this changing climate with intensive focus on writing. Developed by an interdisciplinary, graduate-focused team at Purdue, and now including Michigan State and Arizona, Crow is the first web-based archive which integrate a corpus of student writing with a repository of the pedagogical texts that guide student work. Our project combines humanities approaches to archival methods, qualitative research, and quantitative, data-driven analysis. We consider the changing environments and technologies of writing and the differences in writing practices across speakers from different linguistic and cultural backgrounds. More broadly, our project provides models for sustainable interdisciplinary research and inter-institutional collaboration by thoughtfully engaging graduate and undergraduate researchers in creating digital archives which support new forms of writing research.
nodes.info: **PI**: Bradley Dilger *(Purdue University)* **Project Coordinator**: Bill Hart-Davidson *(Michigan State University)* **Project Consultant**: Shelley Staples *(University of Arizona)*

nodes.label: Political Ecology as Practice
nodes.notes: **Political Ecology as Practice: A Regional Approach to the Anthropocene** This project investigates the reciprocal relationship between the emergent theories of the Anthropocene, climate change, and the global environmental crisis, and how local ecological problems are experienced in various regions of the world. It will address two core questions: (1) do theories generated at the metropolitan center derive insight from regional ecological conflicts? If so, how? (2) Do these theories have an impact on the various communities in terms of their relationship with land, resources, and biodiversity? This project brings together scholars to discuss global theories of the Anthropocene and its new ontologies of time, materiality, and echnology, while investigating their links to regionally specific practices and discourses. It initiates a multi-sited, comparative study of place-based ecological politics through a series of fieldwork initiatives led by faculty and graduate students in collaboration with artists. The fieldwork initiatives are developed from existing projects of collaborating institutions researchers, and involve field observations, visual documentation, interviews, and creative interventions such as public engagement events and art installations. The results of the field initiatives will be presented in public exhibitions, lectures, and publications. Multiple modes of presentation and dissemination will derive inspiration from the innovative format of the field initiatives and collaboration with the arts.
nodes.info: **PI**: Ömür Harmanşah *(University of Illinois Chicago)* **Co-PIs**: Molly Doane *(UIC)*, Ralph Cintron *(UIC)*, Beate Geissler *(UIC)*, David Wise *(UIC)*, Ian Baird *(University of Wisconsin-Madison)*

nodes.label: Garden for a Changing Climate
nodes.notes: **Garden for a Changing Climate** This project is an eight-month presentation of a case-study large scale public art project as the basis through which to examine both the expansion and deepening of an arts-based interdisciplinary undergraduate curriculum and the possibilities for audience co-construction of effective interpretive and educational methods for behavioral change. As a public artwork that makes the shift in ecozones manifest in a large-scale mobile garden, Garden for a Changing Climate addresses the challenge in communicating the climate crisis—that the problem is distant, complex, and uncertain—by making it felt and perceptible. In a collaboration that fuses interdisciplinarity, formal and informal education, museum commissioning and programming, and the creation of a new artwork, Garden for a Changing Climate : A Phenological Clock uses a central effect of climate change to demonstrate how interdisciplinarity across art, science, education, and social science—embedded in every aspect of the project, from the conception of artwork to the museological interpretation of that work to the evaluation of the interpretive strategies—can model pedagogy in an arts-based interdisciplinary undergraduate curriculum and create effective education about the changing climate, its impact on their lives, and how they can join mitigation efforts.
nodes.info: **PI**: Hannah Higgins *(University of Illinois Chicago)* **Co-PI**: Noah Feinstein *(University of Wisconsin-Madison)*

nodes.label: Transmedia Collage
nodes.notes: **Transmedia Collage: Histories of Violence and Futures of Health on Chicago's South Side** This project uses transmedia narrative (a single story told through multiple media and platforms) to reframe research, policy, and public discourse about adolescents on Chicago’s South Side. In collaboration with South Side African American residents, we will generate historical accounts about the past and speculative narratives about possible futures that focus on the ways that a climate of structural violence has impacted the lives of African American adolescent health and wellbeing. This project posits that narrative methods, drawn from humanities disciplines such as history, offer opportunities for research in which power is shared with participants. Along with traditional disciplines, the project contributes to emerging fields such as the public humanities and new media studies.
nodes.info: **PI**: Patrick Jagoda *(University of Chicago)* **Project Coordinator**: Jennifer Brier *(University of Illinois Chicago)* **Creative Director and Producer**: Márquez Rhyne *(UChicago)*

nodes.label: Being Human in the Age of Humans
nodes.notes: **Being Human in the Age of Humans: Perspectives from Religion and Ethics** Discourse on the Anthropocene, which probes the meaning of humanity's role and agency within deep-time, planetary evolution resonates strongly with mythic and religious genres. Anthropocene questions are the purview of religion, philosophy, and ethics. Yet scholarship on the Anthropocene remains underdeveloped in these disciplines, despite their potential to analyze and correct dominant scientific narratives. The Midwest is home to active and sophisticated scholarship on environment, climate change, geoengineering and other topics central to Anthropocene research. By establishing a framework for ongoing collaboration among scholars of religion, theology, philosophy, and ethics at Indiana University, University of Chicago, Michigan State University, and Notre Dame University, the project initiates a second wave of research. Targeting underdeveloped themes of (a) Anthropocene counter-narratives, (b) implicit religion of the Anthropocene, and (c) Indigenous and alternative Antropocene cosmologies, this project will close existing gaps in research and generate new questions. A rigorous and iterative process of selecting and developing outstanding proposals will scale up research. Collaborative workshops and publications will transform isolated pockets of scholarship into a collective enterprise. By nurturing emerging scholars and training students, we will foster new domains of scholarship that will enhance the Midwest's reputation for environental humanities research for years to come.
nodes.info: **PI**: Lisa H. Sideris *(UC Santa Barbara, formerly Indiana University Bloomington)*, **Project Coordinators**: Sarah Fredericks *(University of Chicago)*, Kyle Powys White *(University of Michigan)*, Celia Deane-Drummond *(University of Oxford)*

nodes.label: Hydrologies of the Anthropocene
nodes.notes: **Hydrologies of the Anthropocene: Social Flows and Engineered Watersheds in the Great Lakes Basin** As changes in the climate intensify, waterways and their infrastructures become subject to increasing scrutiny and intervention. The stated motivations are usually to protect vulnerable communities against floods, pollutants, scarcity, and the changing ecologies of water. Approaches to intervention tend to focus on technoscientific fixes, with their attendant epistemological and political-economic assumptions, that end up reproducing the risks in question. Our project hopes to provide a humanistic accounting of waterways and their infrastructures to provide alternative epistemologies, including those of local and diverse communities, and alternative assumptions about economic and political life. “Hydrologies of the Anthropocene: Social Flows and Engineered Watersheds in the Great Lakes Basin” brings together our interest in the contested nature of water infrastructures and discursive representations of waterways, a keen interest in how race, class, and gender relations are embedded in technical apparatuses, and an historical and ethnographic appreciation of the voices of various communities. We employ these sensitivities and build on work in environmental humanities thus far and the humanistic study of rivers in particular to study and reflect on the histories and potential futures of four Rust Belt waterways: The Chicago, Milwaukee, Wolf, and Menominee Rivers.
nodes.info: **PI**: Samer Alatout *(University of Wisconsin-Madison)* **Co-PI**: Rachel Havrelock *(University of Illinois Chicago)*

nodes.label: Arendt on Earth
nodes.notes: **Arendt on Earth: From the Archimedean Point to the Anthropocene** This project takes the elusive concept of "earth" in the thought of Hannah Arendt as a frame, impetus and provocation to "think what we are doing" in the face of multiple, interconnected crises: rapid, unpredictable climate change; the boundlessness of modern production and consumption; the rule of instrumentality over science; fears of technology out of control; the "defactualization" of the world and the corruption of truth in politics; global catastrophes of poverty, displacement, statelessness and rightlessness; and the crises of legitimacy, power, and freedom that face democratic peoples and polities today. Our purpose is not only to foster scholarly engagement with Arendt's writing, but to envision how the humanities can promote public comprehension of the burdens of our time. The project comprised five two-day workshops, each devoted to intensive discussion of papers contributed by invited scholars and project members.
nodes.info: **PI**: Mary G. Dietz *(Northwestern University)* **Project Team**: Dipesh Chakrabarty *(University of Chicago)*, Samantha Frost *(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign)*, Nancy Tuana *(Pennsylvania State University)*, Lexi Neame *(Reed College, formerly Northwestern University)*, Laura Ephraim *(Williams College)*

nodes.label: Field to Media
nodes.notes: **Field to Media: Applied Ethnomusicology for a Changing Climate** Music has often been an important catalyst for social change. Few music scholars, however, have applied their research to help communicate and frame critical environmental questions, despite the increasingly active role the environmental humanities have generally taken in ecological problem solving. This interdisciplinary project draws upon the fields of ecomusicology (ecocritical musicology), praxis-based applied ethnomusicology, and communication studies to create synergy between participatory research, community action, and scholarly publication. Expanding on the effective "field-to-media" methodology piloted by Mark Pedelty in Minnesota, eachmember of the project team will conduct research in one of five environmentally threatened sites around the globe (China, Haiti, India, Tanzania, and Washington State/British Columbia) to gain understanding of how soundscapes help define communities and senses of place and how local musicians creatively mobilize audiences to confront environmental problems. The researchers will each collaborate with their musician-informants to create a music video and social media campaign designed to confront a local environmental challenge. The experiment in creative "soundscaping" promises to generate new theoretical insights into the actual and potential relationships between music, communities, and place. Upon completion of the production phase, the team will publish an open-source field-to-media manual for future practitioners.
nodes.info: **PI**: Mark Pedelty *(University of Minnesota)* **Co-PIs**: Rebecca Dirksen *(Indiana University Bloomington)*, Michael Silvers *(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign)*

nodes.label: The Classroom and the Future of the Historical Record
nodes.notes: **The Classroom and the Future of the Historical Record: Humanities Education in a Changing Climate for Knowledge Production** The conditions under which history is documented are rapidly changing, effected by climatic shifts in how knowledge is produced. New modes of digital communication are creating new ways of capturing, preserving and sharing cultural artifacts, and of using them as evidence of history. Once the preserve of specific memory institutions, publishing the past is a now an activity that plays our across a variety of new media spaces and forms. Under new global conditions of austerity, this digitization of documentary archives has been presented as a boon to humanistic disciplines operating under tightened straits. Yet this turn towards digitizing historical records has also often meant their privatization and commodification. Our project seeks to analyze and explore how higher education’s most basic form of work – teaching – can respond to these two intertwined trends. Our llaboratory—which grows from laboratory experiments being conducted at three leading universities—will explore a range of classroombased documentary processes, from public digitization programs, to the creation of digital documentary editions, to the making of historical quantitative datasets. Our budget combines support for local experiments at each institution as well as funding for collaborative exercises combining faculty, graduate, and undergraduate institutions.
nodes.info: **PI**: John Randolph *(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign)*, **Project Coordinators**: Kathy Oberdeck *(formerly UIUC)*, Daniel Gilbert *(UIUC)*, Bonnie Mak *(UIUC)*, Sharon Leon *(Digital Scholar, formerly Michigan State University)*, Brandon Locke *(MSU)*, William Thomas *(University of Nebraska-Lincoln)*, Patrick Jones *(UNL)*, Aaron Johnson *(UNL)*

nodes.label: Coping with Changing Climates in Early Antiquity
nodes.notes: **Coping with Changing Climates in Early Antiquity: Comparative Approaches between Empiricism and Theory** This project investigates in a comparative perspective the social and cultural perceptions of, and experiences with, climate change in the Bronze and Early Iron Ages in Egypt and Nubia, the Eastern Mediterranean and Anatolia, and Mesopotamia. Addressing a common set of questions through space and time (from Amara to Babylon, and from the third to the early first millennium BCE), it will foster multidisciplinary collaboration between faculty and graduate students specializing in archaeology, bioarchaeology and the study of ancient texts at the three partner institutions. By combining the empirical methods of these Humanistic fields with theories of Socio-Ecological Systems (SES) developed in the fields of Sociology, Political Science and Environmental Studies, it will produce a volume of conference proceedings of the highest academic standards, including a broader outreach towards undergraduate students and other members of the partner institutions (via workshop and poster presentations), and towards the general public (via a dedicated website). It will foster scientific collaboration among the partners and allow graduate students to develop critical research skills (in terms of collaborative work, organization and diffusion), as well as giving them the opportunity to present and publish what will, for most of them, be their first article.
nodes.info: **PI**: Hervé Reculeau *(University of Chicago)* **Project Coordinators**: Michele Buzon *(Purdue University)*, Jay Crisostomo *(University of Michigan)*

nodes.label: Building Collectives in a Changing Healthcare Climate
nodes.notes: **Building Collectives in a Changing Healthcare Climate** The U.S. healthcare system is currently characterized by increasing costs, disparate access to (and quality of) care, and rapidly changing, technologically-mediated processes. In response, healthcare experts have recommended widespread adoption of The Literate Care Model (LCM), which emphasizes preventative care, shared decision-making, and enhanced care coordination, particularly for those patients most affected by health disparities due to social, economic, and environmental factors. Borrowing from the LCM, this project (hereafter, "Building Collectives") emphasizes humanities expertise: rhetorical aptitude; attunement to ethics, access, and equity; multiliteracies; qualitative methods; critical engagement with emergent technologies. Yet, an infrastructure that mobilizes these skills across disciplines and institutions does not yet exist. "Building Collectives" connects humanities scholars with health services researchers in a variety of fields to better enable collaborative scholarship that contributes to improved clinical and public health outcomes. Growing from pre-existing initiatives, we scaffold research teams across the humanities and health sciences, providing humanities researchers with training and support to effectively participate in health services research in clinical settings. Participants in a symposium, educational "grand rounds," online workshops, and asynchronous research teams will develop and share best practices across academy, industry, and community, integrating these through targeted research venues and clinical training.
nodes.info: **PI**: Jacqueline Rhodes *(Michigan State University)* **Co-PIs**: Dawn Opel *(MSU)*, Christa Teston *(The Ohio State University)*, Margaret Price *(OSU)*, John Jones *(OSU)*

nodes.label: Indigenous Art and Activism in Changing Climates
nodes.notes: **Indigenous Art and Activism in Changing Climates: The Mississippi River Valley, Colonialism, and Environmental Change** In this collaborative, interdisciplinary research project, faculty and graduate students combine disciplinary expertise and site resources to study the Mississippi River Valley as a bellwether of changing climates, which Indigenous art and activism harnesses and contests. We focus on both environmental change along the river valley and on changing climates of colonialism, the shifting racial, economic, political, and intellectual climates that have attempted to justify claims to the river valley and re-engineer its flows. Amidst these changing climates, the river valley's Indigenous people create art and resistance that engages the river; they exert their continued rights to their homelands, settlers' claims to land and water and efforts at removal notwithstanding.
nodes.info: **PI**: Kelly Wisecup *(Northwestern University)* **Co-PI**: Vicente Pexa *(University of California Los Angeles, formerly University of Minnesota)* **Project Coordinator**: Christopher Pexa *(University of Minnesota)*

nodes.label: Listening for the Long Haul
nodes.notes:
**Listening for the Long Haul: A Living History of Long COVID** This project partners Long Covid Justice (LCJ), a community-based organization advocating for people living with Long COVID and Associated Conditions (LCAC) led by JD Davids and Gabriel San Emeterio, with History Moves, a public history project led by UIC’s Jennifer Brier, to produce a multifaceted community-centered history of Long COVID. The project asks
how we can use public history methods to shape policies that are more responsive to individual and community needs in the face of pandemics and mass-disabling events and make us all healthier and more resilient. We will train 8 UIC graduate students and 8 LCJ BIPOC community historians in History Moves’ participatory oral history and collective analysis-curation process. Project outcomes include annotated oral
history interviews with 24 community narrators living with LCAC; a collaboratively-produced public-facing digital humanities project; and a digital conversation series to engage and activate diverse stakeholders – long
haulers, health justice activists, humanities scholars, health practitioners and policymakers – to realize Long COVID justice. The personal narratives and historical research will serve as a centerpiece in LCJ’s strategic
vision for creating data-informed communication and narrative strategies, timely patient-led information and perspectives, and supporting communicators living with LCAC.
nodes.info: **PI**: Jennifer Brier *(University of Illinois Chicago)* **Co-PI**: JD Davids *(Network for Long COVID Justice)* **Project Team**: Jennifer Langdon *(Creative Egghead Consulting)*, Gabriel San Emeterio *(Network for Long COVID Justice)*

nodes.label: Maya in the Global Midwest
nodes.notes:
**Maya in the Global Midwest** Over the past 20 years, Maya immigrant communities from Guatemala have transformed
predominantly white rural Midwestern towns in the United States. As these communities have grown, many community members have encountered challenges accessing local public services like schools and healthcare. This project assembles a diverse team of local community organizations from two Midwestern Maya communities - K’iche’, Awakateko, and Ixil speakers in Tuscarawas County, Ohio, and Q’anjob’al speakers in Champaign, Illinois - to document and explore these challenges. The project aims to cultivate a regional network of Maya communities by engaging with community concerns, experiences, and strengths around issues of language
access and language justice. Through a series of workshops, a community-based survey, and
community-driven interviews, we will analyze the ideologies and institutional structures underlying barriers to language access as well as strategies used by Maya communities. We will produce materials that provide a foundation for systemic change including a written public report
aimed towards influencing public policy and work-place practices. While this publicly shareable
knowledge is important, the project’s principal strength lies in its focus on methods that will
build a network of relationships and tools that allow the community to pursue and mobilize new resources into the future.
nodes.info: **PI**: Laura Horton *(University of Wisconsin-Madison)* **Project Team**: María Luz García *(Eastern Michigan University)*, Miguel Guzaro Raymundo *(Ixil Community Leader)*, Ana Floridalma Lucas Mateo *(Pixan Konob' Q'anjob'al Language Justice Collective)*, Korinta Maldonado *(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign)*, Nathalie Martinez *(UIUC)*, Sherrel Rieger *(Puentes)*, Maria Solis López *(Ixil Interpreter)*, Manuela Peña *(Immigrant Worker Project)*, Daniel Baltazar Gregorio Juan *(Pixan Konob' Q'anjob'al Language Justice Collective)*, Gloria Yen *(New American Welcome Center at UIUC YMCA)*

nodes.label: The Flint Water Disaster Public Archive
nodes.notes:
**The Flint Water Disaster Public Archive** This project
seeks to enact “data justice” for public records relating to the Flint Water Crisis. It is a collaborative extension of an ongoing project--creating an online archive of
455,000 PDF pages of relevant government emails and related public digital documents. Over
the next two years, project participants will form a Community Research Collective, convening academic researchers, archival staff, and local community experts. This collective will collaborate to develop consensus on key issues relating to the water disaster; set specific goals around political education; discuss and shape research directions; determine the right methods and designs to accomplish our goals, and execute those goals. Material products created during the grant period will include two website exhibits of archival data and a related “guidebook” or atlas contextualizing the online archive in terms of water politics. Through iterative methods
including timeline construction and critical narrative analysis, we aim to conduct a different form
of “citizen science” that centers community members as political experts. Our project aims to “re-home” data of urgent relevance to Flint, largely produced about the city by state actors, and little seen by residents.
nodes.info: **PI**: Louise Seamster *(University of Iowa) **Co-PI**: Andrew Herscher *(University of Michigan)* **Collaborators**: Claire McClinton *(Flint Democracy Defense League)*, Monica Lewis-Patrick *(We the People of Detroit)*, Callum Carr *(University of Michigan-Flint)*, Chad Rhym *(U Iowa)*, Hannah Zadeh *(U Iowa)*, Bee Rinaldi *(U Iowa), Abett Smith *(UMich)*, Matthew Butler *(U Iowa)*, Tom Keegan *(U Iowa)*

nodes.label: Archival Repatriation and Boarding School Healing
nodes.notes:
**Archival Repatriation and Boarding School Healing: The Morris Indian Industrial School and White Earth Nation** Between 1887 and 1909, hundreds of Anishinaabe people from the White Earth Reservation in northern Minnesota were sent to a boarding school in Morris, Minnesota—first run by the
Catholic Church, and later the federal government. This project will bring together the Niibi Center, a White Earth-based non-profit with expertise in boarding school healing, with graduate
students, undergraduates, and faculty at the University of Minnesota, Morris and the University of Wisconsin-Madison to repatriate electronic copies of records from the Morris Indian School held at the National Archives in Washington, D.C. It will work in three phases: First, we will offer community members from White Earth access to archival documents related to their ancestors that have been rendered inaccessible by travel costs and protocols of colonial archives. Working with the Niibi Center, we will evaluate these documents for repatriation to the White Earth Nation Tribal Archives and assist in incorporating them into ongoing community-based programs for boarding school healing. Finally, students and faculty will listen to White Earth community members about how boarding school histories might be represented in curriculum and campus life. We hope to provide a model for reciprocity and collaboration between institutions of higher education and tribal nations.
nodes.info: **PI**: Kevin Whalen *(University of Minnesota)* **Co-PI**: Becca Gercken *(UMN)* **Project Archivist**: Steve Gross *(UMN)* **Project Coordinator**: Matthew Villeneuve *(University of Wisconsin-Madison)*

nodes.label: Black Study and Creative Praxis in the Greater Midwest
nodes.notes:
**Black Study and Creative Praxis in the Greater Midwest** The Black Midwest Initiative, which is housed in the Department of Black Studies at the University
of Illinois Chicago, is a collective of people within and beyond the university who are working
toward the liberation of Black people living throughout the greater Midwest region of the United States. This project supports the development of a pilot Summer Institute to take place at UIC in 2023 during which fifteen emerging scholars, artists, and organizers will develop projects in consultation with established scholars and practitioners in their fields that will be shown or exhibited in Dayton, Ohio during the Third Biennial Black Midwest Symposium in 2024. This project also supports two summer retreats to take place in 2023 and 2024 during which BMI members will work toward the development of an edited book, Black in the Middle: An Anthology of the Black Midwest: Volume II, and a corresponding digital exhibition that will feature contributors to the symposium and the Summer Institute, as well as a broader cross-section of contributors from the region. This proposal is a collaboration between the Black Midwest Initiative; Dayton Contemporary Dance Company; Sinclair Community College of Dayton, Ohio; Dayton Metro Library; Belt Publishing; and the literary journal and digital platform Obsidian Literature &
Arts in the African Diaspora.
nodes.info: **PI**: Terrion Williamson *(University of Illinois Chicago)* **Project Collaborators**: Kandise Bobo *(Sinclair Community College)*, Angela Burdon *(Dayton Contemporary Dance Company)*, Debi Chess *(Dayton Metro Library)*, Tama Hamilton-Wray *(Michigan State University)*, Rodney Veal *(Sinclair Community College)*

nodes.label: Communiversities as Education Without Walls
nodes.notes: **Communiversities as Education Without Walls: Building Coalitions for Liberatory Education Through the Humanities** This project will create communiversities (community-based, people-centered popular educational spaces) in three midwestern cities (Chicago, Cincinnati, and Detroit) with long histories of educational enclosure and social movement organizing. In total, the three communiversity sites will bring together close to 60 K-12 students, community activists, and P-20 educators, who will engage in inquiry-to-action projects, co-designed and co-led by teams of university faculty, leaders at community-based organizations, and youth.
nodes.info: **PI**: Asif Wilson *(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign)* **Co-PIs**: Rachel McMillian *(Indiana University Indianapolis, formerly UIUC)*, Aja Reynolds *(Wayne State University)*

nodes.label: Environmental Justice Worldmaking
nodes.notes:
**Environmental Justice Worldmaking: Redistribution and Reciprocity for a Just Transition** This project creates Environmental Justice Worldmaking (EJW) domains based on overarching Environmental Justice principles and commitments to antiracism, direct democracy, and a just transition. EJW anchors cross-institutional and community-engaged collaboration that centers ways that the humanities
and humanistic social sciences can affect the just transformation of democracy. We will develop an innovative model of Environmental Justice research, programming, and curriculum guided by grassroots activism and carried out in the spirit of collaboration, redistribution, and reciprocity. EJW recasts how we respond to the needs of local people contending with everyday struggles and violences being done to the environment, which are tightly bound up. The Institute for Redistributive and Regenerative Life will hold these domains. It serves as a node that connects Atlanta and Minneapolis; two institutions of higher education, the University of Minnesota, a public research university, and Spelman College, a Historically Black liberal arts college for women; and community-based organizations in these two cities that operate on a translocal scale, the Environmental Justice Health Alliance and the Minnesota
Environmental Justice Table. With the involvement of graduate students throughout the process, EJW scales up to become a movement-building space, platform-making, an epistemology, and praxis.
nodes.info: **PI**: Rose Brewer *(University of Minnesota)* **Co-PI**: Tania Mitchell *(UMN)* **Project Team**: Fatemeh Shafei *(Spelman College)*, Yuichiro Onishi *(UMN)*, Michele Roberts *(Environmental Justice Health Alliance for Chemical Policy)*, Nazir Khan *(Minnesota Environmental Justice Table)*, Karen Brown *(UMN)*

nodes.label: Black Trans in the Americas
nodes.notes:
**Black Trans in the Americas** This project is a community-based and community-led research partnership that
aims to document and celebrate the myriad of ways that Black Trans people survive, create
community, build programs, lead movements and make indelible marks in the Americas. There is
an urgent need for explicit attention to Black Trans lived experience, in the face of increased transphobic violence and anti-trans legislation across geographies. Humanities scholarship is necessary for this project as it is attuned to narration, translation, and representation as modalities, methods, and forms, but also as reflective of power relations. Our goal is to create a sustainable, web-based BTiA network and archive of community-based interviews, oral histories, films, and other creative outputs built by and for Black Trans communities. Taking the
humanities outside the walls of universities by using digital arts and media to connect audiences
across national borders, we can cultivate networks of knowledge and care among communities
historically excluded by our institutions. We will expand interest and participation in humanistic inquiry, transforming individuals and communities from objects of study to stewards of their own histories and stories. This project builds on a broader partnership between Northwestern University, University of Chicago, the community-based organization OTV | Open Television, along with universities and organizations globally.
nodes.info: **PI**: Aymar Jéan Christian *(Northwestern University)* **Co-PI**: Riley Snorton *(University of Chicago)* **Project Coordinator**: Jamie Cooley *(Northwestern University)*

nodes.label: Reclaiming Stories
nodes.notes: **Reclaiming Stories: (Re)connecting Indigenous Painted Hides to Communities through Collaborative Conversations** Extraordinary artworks made by Indigenous peoples of North American prairies in the 17th and 18th centuries reside today in a large collection of American materials culture in French institutions. Guided by Indigenous methodologies, ethics of collaborative research, and a spirit of reciprocity and redistribution, this project creates a significant opportunity for members of the Peewaalia and Myaamia communities—historians, artists, cultural officers, and students—to reconnect with these objects and reclaim their meanings. Building on extraordinary ongoing efforts among Myaamia and Peewalia communities to recover cultural traditions, for instance through language revitalization and artistic awakening, this project reconnects tribal knowledge-makers to objects/beings that have long been inaccessible owing to location and to institutional attitudes in the museum and academic worlds that often ignored Indigenous voices. Seizing the opportunity created by a new interpretive initiative within the Musée du Quai Branly, this project will result in a public history project for tribal and larger audiences, culminating in an exhibition. This work will also lead to, at least, a hybrid/digital exhibition at the Miami University Museum of Art. A possible future or concurrent Phase II would fund—in partnership with the Musée du Quai Branly—a collaborative exhibition that would actually bring their extraordinary artworks to North America, ideally to Myaamia and Peewaalia homelands.
nodes.info: **PI**: Robert Morrissey *(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign)* **Project Team**: Madison Bastress *(New York University)*, David Costa *(Myaamia Center)*, Charla Echohawk *(Peoria Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma)*, Elizabeth Ellis *(NYU, Peoria Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma)*, Wesley Farless *(Peoria Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma)*, Jack Green *(Miami University Art Museum)*, George Ironstack *(Myaamia Center, Miami Tribe of Oklahoma)*, Logan Pappenfort *(Illinois State Museum, Peoria Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma)*, Jason Shaiman *(Miami University Art Museum)*, Scott Shoemaker *(Cargill Foundation, Miami Tribe of Oklahoma)*, Cam Shriver *(Myaamia Center, Miami University)*

nodes.label: Amplifying Mothers of Police Violence Survivors
nodes.notes: **Amplifying Mothers of Police Violence Survivors** This project grew out of a two-year process of relationship building between the P.I. and a collective of Black and Latinx mothers who call themselves "Mothers of the Kidnapped" (MOK). Their children were physically or mentally abused and wrongfully convicted by Chicago police. The research asks: *How can advocacy led by MOK members help address the devastating losses these mothers endure "on the outside" of prison walls while simultaneously contributing to efforts seeking justice for police survivors "on the inside?"* Through a reciprocal and redistributive methodology, "Amplifying" supports MOK members in advocating for wrongfully convicted individuals. It simultaneously explores the theoretical significance of mother-led activism to prison reform and abolition. MOK members have co-designed this project, including three advocacy campaigns they will lead. "Amplifying" relies upon a reproductive justice framework to build up communities of advocacy and care while blurring the boundaries of "inside" and "outside" prison walls that often frame justice advocacy and research. In doing so, it will (1) expand definitions of "victim/survivor" of the carceral state beyond masculinist approaches that prioritize men inmates living "on the inside" and (2) contribute an expansive framework that can address the needs and struggles of all victims/survivors. "Amplifying" culminates in the publication of a book.
nodes.info: **PI**: Nadine Naber *(University of Illinois Chicago)* **Partners**: Souzan Naser *(Mamas Activating Movements for Abolition and Solidarity)*, Johnaé Strong *(MAMAS)*, Joey Mogul *(People's Law Office)*, Yesenia Vargas *(UIC)*

nodes.label: The Latinx Obstetric Violence Project
nodes.notes: **The Latinx Obstetric Violence Project: Art and Literature as Tools of Reciprocal and Redistributive Knowledge** Maternity care reproduces persistent, historical inequalities, and inequities associated with race, class, gender, and ethnicity. In partnership with community leaders and organizations such as La Casa de Armistad, graduate students, and members of the Latinx community in South Bend, Indiana, this project addresses the overlooked reality of obstetric violence through a series of art and literature workshops. The goal for this collaborative, reciprocal research project is to bring together women, scholars, and artists (writers, painters, photographers) who have engaged with and portrayed violence against women in childbirth. The artists' works in literature and the visual arts can facilitate deeper knowledge of harm, healing, and prevention in the community and around obstetric violence. The goal is to co-create a space for women to engage in workshops and share their experiences artistically (through poems, short essays, drawings, paintings, embroidery, etc.), which will conclude in an exhibit based on the women's artistic representations. Knowledge and awareness about the subject of obstetric violence needs to be built in a reciprocal and shared process to elicit an open, powerful, and raw conversation about women, birth, and violence.
nodes.info: **PI**: Vania Smith-Oka *(University of Notre Dame)* **Co-PI**: Vanesa Miseres *(University of Notre Dame)* **Project Team**: Simona Spiegel *(Notre Dame)*, Ignacio Sánchez Osores *(Notre Dame)*
